etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English moste ("must", literally, "had to", the past tense of Middle English moten (“to have to”)), from Old English mōste (“had to”), 1st & 3rd person singular past tense of mōtan (“to be allowed, be able to, have the opportunity to, be compelled to, must, may”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtaną. Cognate with Dutch moest (“had to”), German musste (“had to”), Swedish måste (“must, have to, be obliged to”). More at mote.

definitions.definition: (modal auxiliary, defective) To do as a requirement; indicates that the sentence subject is required as an imperative or directive to execute the sentence predicate, with failure to do so resulting in a failure or negative consequence.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Acts 9:6:
quote.text: Arise, and go into the city, and it shall be told thee what thou must do.

definitions.definition: (modal auxiliary, defective) To do with certainty; indicates that the speaker is certain that the subject will have executed the predicate.

You picked one of two, and it wasn't the: it must have been the second.

definitions.definition: (modal auxiliary, defective) Used to indicate that something is very likely, probable, or certain to be true.
Something that is mandatory or required.

quote.citation: 1932, Helen Vinson, I Am a Fugitive from a Chain Gang:
quote.text: "There are no musts in my life - I'm free, white, and twenty-one."

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English must, from Old English must and Old French must, most, both from Latin mustum.

definitions.definition: The property of being stale or musty.
Something that exhibits the property of being stale or musty.
Fruit juice that will ferment or has fermented, usually from grapes.

quote.citation: c. 1874, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Ovid in Exile:
quote.text: No sweet grape lies hidden here in the shade of its vine-leaves,No fermenting must fills and o'erflows the deep vats.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Persian مست (mast, “drunk, inebriated”), from Middle Persian 𐭬𐭮𐭲 (mast).

quote.citation: 1936, George Orwell, Shooting an Elephant, an essay in the magazine New Writing:
quote.text: It was not, of course, a wild elephant, but a tame one which had gone ‘must’.
